newsitem.title: UK: ICCO sees cocoa deficit at 225,000 T in 1996/97.
newsitem.headline: ICCO sees cocoa deficit at 225,000 T in 1996/97.

text.p: The International Cocoa Organization (ICCO) secretariat has forecast a world cocoa deficit of 225,000 tonnes in 1996/97 (Oct/Sept) compared with an estimated surplus of 133,000 tonnes in 1995/96.

It pegged the total Ivorian output at 1.0 million tonnes from 1.2 million in the last season while total world production was forecast at a gross 2.622 million tonnes, down from a revised 1995/96 estimate of 2.900 million.
Grindings were put at 2.821 million tonnes, up from a revised 2.738 million last season.
The production balance is calculated by subtracting one pct from gross output to allow for loss in weight and then deducting grindings.

The ICCO said total statistical cocoa bean stocks at the end of 1996/97 should decline to 1.162 million tonnes, from an estimated 1.404 million in 1995/96. This would be equivalent to 41.2 percent or almost five months of projected annual world grindings in 1996/97.
Excluding the buffer stocks of 26,000 tonnes, total stocks directly overhanging the market would amount to 1.136 million tonnes, also about five months of estimated grindings.
The ICCO forecast output in Ghana at 330,000 tonnes, down almost 70,000 tonnes from a revised 1995/96 estimate.
Brazil was put at 195,000 tonnes, down from 230,000, Nigeria was down to 140,000 from a revised 147,000 and Cameroon was seen at 120,000 tonnes against a revised 130,000.
In the Far East, Indonesia and Malaysia were seen producing higher crops at 330,000 and 120,000 tonnes respectively.
Total grindings were seen at a new all-time high with a rise of 10,000 tonnes in the Netherlands to 395,000 tonnes, marginally offset by lower German and UK figures. U.S. grindings were also seen up.
Grindings in Ivory Coast were expected to reach 160,000 tonnes, up 20,000, and smaller increases were seen in other African origins in line with a shift of processing from consumer countries.
